definition: The science of sound: how it is produced, travels through air and materials, reflects, is absorbed and is heard. In audio engineering it covers speakers, rooms and microphones.
example: Room acoustics explains why the same speaker sounds boomy in a small bare room and fine in a treated studio.

definition: The small, rapid rise and fall of air pressure above and below the steady atmospheric pressure caused by a sound wave. It is measured in pascals (Pa), usually as an RMS value.
example: A loud conversation is roughly 0.02 Pa of sound pressure, on top of about 101,325 Pa of atmospheric pressure.

definition: Sound pressure expressed in decibels relative to 20 µPa, the approximate threshold of hearing at 1 kHz: SPL = 20·log10(p / 20 µPa). It is the standard way to say how loud a sound is physically.
example: 1 Pa is about 94 dB SPL; 20 Pa is 120 dB SPL.

definition: The SI unit of pressure: one newton of force per square metre. Sound pressures are tiny fractions of a pascal to tens of pascals.
example: 1 Pa of sound pressure corresponds to about 94 dB SPL.

definition: One millionth of a pascal. The reference pressure for dB SPL is 20 µPa, roughly the quietest 1 kHz tone a young listener can hear.
example: 20 µPa = 0.00002 Pa = 0 dB SPL.

definition: The steady pressure of the air around us, about 101,325 Pa at sea level. Sound is a tiny ripple on top of it.
example: Even a painfully loud 120 dB SPL sound is only a 20 Pa ripple on 101,325 Pa.

definition: The part of a sound wave where the air is slightly thinner (lower pressure) than normal, opposite to a compression, where it is squeezed. A sound wave is alternating compressions and rarefactions.
example: A speaker cone moving backwards leaves a rarefaction in front of it.

definition: A wave in which the medium moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels, rather than across it. Sound in air is longitudinal.
example: Air molecules in front of a speaker jiggle towards and away from the listener as the sound passes.

definition: How fast sound travels through a medium. In dry air it depends mainly on temperature: about 331 m/s at 0 °C and 343 m/s at 20 °C, roughly 1 metre every 2.9 ms.
example: Sound takes about 117 ms to travel 40 m at 20 °C.

definition: The SI unit of speed: how many metres something travels each second.
example: Sound in air at 20 °C travels at about 343 m/s.

definition: An environment with no reflecting surfaces, so sound travels only directly from the source. Outdoors high above the ground, or in an anechoic chamber, approximates it.
example: Speaker sensitivity is ideally measured in a free field so the room does not change the result.

definition: In a free field, sound from a small source spreads over a sphere, so intensity falls with the square of distance and pressure falls in proportion to distance. Each doubling of distance loses about 6 dB.
example: A speaker giving 100 dB SPL at 1 m gives about 94 dB at 2 m and 80 dB at 10 m outdoors.

definition: The sound power flowing through each square metre, in watts per square metre (W/m²). It is proportional to sound pressure squared.
example: Doubling the sound pressure multiplies the intensity by four.

definition: The region close to a sound source where different parts of the source are at noticeably different distances, so their contributions interfere and level does not fall neatly at 6 dB per doubling of distance.
example: Moving a measurement microphone a few centimetres near a large cabinet can change the level sharply.

definition: The region far enough from a source that it behaves like a point: level falls about 6 dB per doubling of distance and the balance between drivers stays steady.
example: Datasheet sensitivities at 1 m are often measured further away in the far field and scaled back.

definition: The part of the sound in a room made of many overlapping reflections. Far from the source it is roughly the same level everywhere, so the level stops falling with distance.
example: At the back of a hall, most of what you hear is the reverberant field rather than the direct sound.

definition: The distance from a source in a room at which the direct sound and the reverberant sound are equally loud. Closer than this, direct sound dominates; further away, the room dominates.
example: In a lively room the critical distance may be only a couple of metres.

definition: Sound sources whose waveforms are unrelated, such as two separate noise sources. Their powers add, so two equal ones give +3 dB.
example: Two identical air-conditioning units at 50 dB each give about 53 dB together.

definition: Sources playing the same signal with a fixed time relationship, such as two speakers fed one channel. Their pressures add, giving up to +6 dB where they arrive in phase and cancellation where they are out of phase.
example: Two speakers playing the same bass note equidistant from you can give +6 dB.

definition: The series of regularly spaced peaks and notches in frequency response caused by adding a signal to a delayed copy of itself. The plotted response looks like the teeth of a comb.
example: A reflection delayed by 1 ms causes notches at 500 Hz, 1.5 kHz, 2.5 kHz and so on.

definition: What happens when two waves overlap: they add where they are in step (constructive) and cancel where they are opposite (destructive).
example: Two speakers playing one tone create spots of loud and quiet as you walk across the room.

definition: Two signals are in phase when their peaks line up, so they reinforce; out of phase (180° apart) when one's peak meets the other's trough, so they cancel.
example: Reversing the polarity of one of two identical speakers puts them out of phase and the bass largely disappears.

definition: The fraction of sound energy a surface absorbs instead of reflecting, from 0 (perfect reflector) to 1 (absorbs everything). It varies with frequency and is written α (alpha).
example: A thick mineral-wool panel may have α ≈ 0.9 at 1 kHz but much less at 100 Hz.

definition: The conversion of sound energy into heat by a material, so less is reflected back into the room. Porous materials absorb by friction as air moves through them.
example: Mineral wool panels at first-reflection points absorb mids and highs.

definition: A mirror-like reflection from a large, flat, hard surface, where the angle in equals the angle out. It works well only when the surface is large compared with the wavelength.
example: A bare side wall gives a strong specular reflection of a monitor's treble.

definition: The bending of waves around obstacles and spreading through openings. Sound diffracts strongly when the obstacle is small compared with its wavelength.
example: You hear the bass but not the cymbals of a band round a corner because long bass wavelengths diffract.

definition: A region behind an obstacle where sound is quieter because the obstacle blocks it. It only forms for wavelengths that are small compared with the obstacle.
example: Your head casts an acoustic shadow at 5 kHz but hardly any at 200 Hz.

definition: The fixed ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159. It appears in acoustics formulas involving circles, spheres and cycles (2π radians per cycle).
example: A sphere of radius r has surface area 4πr².

definition: The Greek letter lambda, used as the symbol for wavelength: the distance a wave travels during one cycle, λ = c/f.
example: At 1 kHz in air, λ = 343 / 1000 ≈ 0.34 m.

definition: The Greek letter alpha. In this module it stands for an absorption coefficient in room acoustics, and for the compliance ratio Vas/Vb in sealed-box design.
example: α = 0.9 means a surface absorbs 90% of the sound energy hitting it.

definition: Frequency measured in radians per second instead of cycles per second: ω = 2π × f. Filter maths is usually written in ω. In normalised filter maths, such as the crossover lesson's, ω is instead the frequency divided by the crossover frequency, with no unit.
example: 1 kHz is ω ≈ 6283 rad/s.

definition: log10(x) answers "10 to what power gives x?". Decibels use it to turn huge ratios into manageable numbers.
example: log10(100) = 2, so a power ratio of 100 is 10 × 2 = 20 dB.

definition: The SI unit of solid angle: how much of the space around a point something covers. A full sphere is 4π steradians and a half-space (in front of a wall) is 2π.
example: A speaker on a large baffle radiates into 2π steradians at high frequencies.

definition: A source radiating into the hemisphere in front of a large surface (half-space, 2π) gets the same energy into half the area, so about +6 dB more pressure on-axis than radiating into full space (4π).
example: A subwoofer moved from mid-room onto the floor radiates into half-space at low frequencies.

definition: A simplified model of a gas whose molecules do not attract each other. It predicts that the speed of sound in air rises with absolute temperature.
example: The ideal-gas model gives 343 m/s at 20 °C.

definition: The study of how people perceive sound: loudness, pitch, direction and timbre, as opposed to the physical pressure a meter measures.
example: Masking and equal-loudness contours are psychoacoustic effects.

definition: A curve joining the sound pressure levels at which pure tones of different frequencies sound equally loud. They show that bass needs much more SPL to sound as loud as mid frequencies, especially at low levels. The first were published by Fletcher and Munson in 1933.
example: On the 40-phon contour of ISO 226:2003, a 100 Hz tone needs about 64 dB SPL to sound as loud as a 40 dB SPL tone at 1 kHz.

definition: The unit of loudness level. A sound is n phons if it sounds as loud as a 1 kHz tone at n dB SPL.
example: Every point on the 80-phon contour sounds as loud as 80 dB SPL at 1 kHz.

definition: The international standard that defines normal equal-loudness contours for pure tones. It replaced the older curves in 2003 and was revised again in 2023.
example: Read real equal-loudness values from ISO 226 rather than from sketches.

definition: The International Organization for Standardization, which publishes international standards such as ISO 226 for equal-loudness contours.
example: ISO 226 defines the equal-loudness contours used in acoustics.

definition: The International Electrotechnical Commission, which publishes international standards for electrical and electronic equipment, including sound level meters (IEC 61672), loudspeakers (IEC 60268-5) and phantom power (IEC 61938).
example: IEC 61938 defines P48 phantom power.

definition: The international standard for sound level meters, which defines the A, C and Z frequency weightings and the meters' accuracy classes.
example: A class 1 meter meets the tighter IEC 61672-1 tolerances.

definition: An instrument with a calibrated microphone that measures sound pressure level, usually with selectable A, C or Z frequency weighting and time averaging.
example: Venue engineers keep a sound level meter at front of house to track dB(A) and dB(C).

definition: A filter applied to a sound measurement to make one number track human response or a measurement purpose. The common ones are A, C and Z weighting.
example: The same noise can read 70 dB(A) and 85 dB(C) if it is mostly bass.

definition: A frequency weighting that strongly reduces low frequencies (about −19 dB at 100 Hz, −30 dB at 50 Hz) and slightly boosts 2–4 kHz, roughly following the ear at low levels. Levels measured with it are written dB(A) or dBA; it is the standard for noise exposure.
example: A 50 Hz tone at 90 dB SPL reads only about 60 dB(A).

definition: A frequency weighting that is nearly flat from about 31.5 Hz to 8 kHz. It is used for peak measurements and for loud, bass-heavy sound that A-weighting would under-read.
example: Workplace peak limits in Great Britain are given in dB(C).

definition: A flat ("zero") frequency weighting: the measurement is not filtered across the specified range.
example: A Z-weighted reading includes all the sub-bass that A-weighting removes.

definition: When one sound makes another harder or impossible to hear. It is strongest for sounds close in frequency and spreads upwards: loud low sounds mask higher ones more than the reverse.
example: A loud bass line can make a quiet pad in the same octave disappear.

definition: Masking of a sound by another playing at the same time, strongest when the two are close in frequency.
example: Two synth parts in the same register mask each other in a mix.

definition: Masking across time: a loud sound hides quieter sounds just after it (forward masking) and, briefly, just before it (backward masking).
example: A quiet tick right after a loud snare hit may not be heard.

definition: Software that compresses audio by throwing away information predicted to be inaudible, often using masking. MP3 and AAC are examples. Decoding does not restore the original exactly.
example: A 128 kbit/s MP3 is about one eleventh the size of CD-quality audio.

definition: A widely used lossy audio format (MPEG-1/2 Audio Layer III) that uses a psychoacoustic model to discard sound that masking makes inaudible.
example: A 320 kbit/s MP3 is often hard to tell from the original.

definition: Advanced Audio Coding: a lossy audio format designed as a successor to MP3, usually giving better quality at the same bit rate. It is used by Apple Music and YouTube.
example: AAC at 256 kbit/s is the iTunes Store standard.

definition: The spiral, fluid-filled organ of the inner ear that turns sound vibrations into nerve signals. Different positions along it respond to different frequencies, so it acts like a bank of filters.
example: Hair cells near the base of the cochlea respond to high frequencies and are often damaged first by noise.

definition: The range of frequencies around a tone within which other sounds strongly interact with it in the ear (masking, beating, roughness). Bands are narrow at low frequencies and wider at high ones.
example: Two bass notes 20 Hz apart fall in the same critical band and fight each other.

definition: The width of an ideal rectangular filter that passes the same total power as an auditory filter with the same peak. Glasberg and Moore's formula, ERB = 24.7 × (4.37 × f/1000 + 1) Hz, gives about 133 Hz at 1 kHz.
example: At 100 Hz the ERB is only about 36 Hz.

definition: A filter that passes a range of frequencies around a centre frequency and reduces those above and below it.
example: The cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters.

definition: How the brain works out where a sound comes from, using time and level differences between the ears and the filtering of the outer ear.
example: You can point to a person speaking behind you with your eyes shut thanks to localisation.

definition: The difference in arrival time of a sound at the two ears. It is the main left–right cue below about 1 kHz; the maximum for an adult head is of order 0.6–0.7 ms.
example: A sound from your far right reaches your right ear about 0.6 ms before your left.

definition: The difference in level of a sound at the two ears, caused by the head's acoustic shadow. It is the main left–right cue at high frequencies, above about 1.5 kHz.
example: A 6 kHz tone from the side can be 10 dB or more louder at the near ear.

definition: Lord Rayleigh's 1907 explanation of left–right localisation: time differences dominate at low frequencies and level differences at high frequencies.
example: Duplex theory explains why ITD matters for bass and ILD for treble.

definition: The visible outer ear. Its folds filter sound differently depending on direction, which helps the brain tell front from back and up from down.
example: Sounds above you are coloured differently by the pinna than sounds in front.

definition: The auditory system's tendency to localise a sound by its first-arriving wavefront and suppress the direction of reflections that arrive soon after. Described in detail by Helmut Haas around 1949–51.
example: Delay speakers rely on the precedence effect so the sound still seems to come from the stage.

definition: The leading edge of a sound wave as it spreads out from a source.
example: The direct sound's wavefront arrives before any reflection.

definition: Permanent hearing damage caused by exposure to loud sound, depending on both level and duration (the noise dose). It usually affects 3–6 kHz first.
example: Years of unprotected loud rehearsals can cause noise-induced hearing loss.

definition: Hearing a ringing, hissing or buzzing sound that has no outside source. Temporary tinnitus after loud music is a warning sign of over-exposure.
example: Ringing ears after a gig mean you received a high noise dose.

definition: The combined effect of sound level and exposure time on hearing risk. With a 3 dB exchange rate, 3 dB louder for half as long gives the same dose.
example: 85 dB(A) for 8 hours and 88 dB(A) for 4 hours are the same NIOSH dose.

definition: How many decibels of extra level halve the allowed exposure time. NIOSH uses 3 dB, which follows equal-energy reasoning.
example: At 3 dB exchange rate, 94 dB(A) is allowed for 1 hour if 85 dB(A) is allowed for 8.

aliases: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
definition: The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Its recommended exposure limit for noise is 85 dB(A) averaged over 8 hours with a 3 dB exchange rate.
example: Under NIOSH guidance, 100 dB(A) reaches a full day's dose in 15 minutes.

definition: A NIOSH limit on workplace exposure. For noise it is 85 dB(A) as an 8-hour time-weighted average.
example: The NIOSH REL is stricter than the US legal OSHA limit of 90 dB(A).

definition: The Health and Safety Executive, Great Britain's workplace health and safety regulator. It enforces the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005.
example: HSE guidance INDG362 summarises the noise action values.

term: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005
definition: The Great Britain law setting workplace noise action values (80 and 85 dB(A) daily, 135 and 137 dB(C) peak) and limits (87 dB(A), 140 dB(C)). It applies to music and entertainment work.
example: At 85 dB(A) daily exposure, hearing protection becomes mandatory.

definition: A noise level in the Control of Noise at Work Regulations at which an employer must act. In Great Britain the lower is 80 dB(A) (135 dB(C) peak) and the upper 85 dB(A) (137 dB(C) peak).
example: Above the upper action value, hearing protection zones must be marked.

definition: The noise level that must never be exceeded in Great Britain workplaces: 87 dB(A) daily/weekly or 140 dB(C) peak. Unlike the action values, it takes account of hearing protection worn.
example: Ear defenders can bring a worker's exposure below the 87 dB(A) limit value.

definition: A person's A-weighted noise exposure over a working day, expressed as the steady level that would give the same energy over 8 hours. LEP,w is the weekly average equivalent.
example: 4 hours at 88 dB(A) gives an LEP,d of about 85 dB(A).

definition: The highest instantaneous C-weighted sound pressure level, used for limits on impulsive noise such as gunshots or snare hits.
example: The Great Britain upper peak action value is 137 dB(C).

definition: The equivalent continuous A-weighted sound level: the steady level with the same total energy as the varying sound over a stated period.
example: WHO recommends audiences get no more than 100 dB LAeq over any 15 minutes.

definition: The World Health Organization, the UN agency for health. It publishes safe-listening standards for personal audio devices (with ITU) and for venues and events.
example: The WHO venue standard sets a 100 dB LAeq,15 min ceiling.

definition: The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for telecommunications standards. With WHO it published the safe-listening standard for personal audio devices.
example: The WHO–ITU standard allows 80 dB for 40 hours a week for adults.

definition: A fast compressor with a very high ratio that stops a signal going above a set level. Used to protect speakers and ears.
example: A limiter on your monitoring path stops a bug in your synth code sending a full-scale square wave to your headphones.

definition: Earplugs with a filter designed to reduce level fairly evenly across frequency, so music sounds quieter but not muffled. Common filter ratings are about 9, 15 and 25 dB.
example: A drummer with 15 dB musicians' earplugs still hears a balanced band.

definition: A transducer that turns sound pressure into an electrical voltage. Dynamic, condenser and ribbon are the main types.
example: A vocal mic delivers a few millivolts for normal singing.

definition: A device that converts energy from one form to another, such as sound to voltage (a microphone) or voltage to sound (a loudspeaker).
example: Microphones and speakers are both transducers.

definition: A microphone in which a coil attached to the diaphragm moves in a magnetic field and generates a voltage by electromagnetic induction. Rugged, needs no power, but has low output.
example: A Shure SM58 is a dynamic microphone giving about 1.9 mV/Pa.

definition: A microphone in which the diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor; sound changes the gap and so the voltage. It needs power for its internal electronics and is usually sensitive and detailed.
example: A Neumann U 87 Ai is a large-diaphragm condenser microphone.

definition: A microphone using a thin corrugated metal ribbon suspended in a magnetic field; sound moves the ribbon, generating a voltage. Naturally figure-8, smooth-sounding and fragile.
example: A blast of air from a kick-drum port can stretch a ribbon.

definition: The thin, light membrane in a microphone or speaker that moves with sound pressure. In a loudspeaker it is the cone or dome that pushes the air.
example: A condenser's diaphragm may be just a few micrometres thick.

definition: The generation of a voltage in a conductor moving through a magnetic field (or in a changing field). It is how dynamic and ribbon mics, and speakers acting as generators, produce voltage.
example: Moving a voice coil in its magnet gap generates a voltage proportional to its speed.

definition: The fixed, perforated plate behind a condenser microphone's diaphragm, forming the other plate of the capacitor.
example: Sound pushing the diaphragm towards the backplate increases the capacitance.

definition: A material that holds a permanent electric charge, used in many condenser mics instead of an external polarising voltage. Electret mics still need power for their impedance converter.
example: Most phone and laptop mics are electret capsules.

definition: The fixed DC voltage that charges a true condenser microphone capsule so that changes in capacitance produce a signal voltage.
example: Many phantom-powered studio condensers, such as the Neumann U 87 Ai, generate a capsule polarising voltage of about 60 V from phantom power with an internal DC-to-DC converter.

definition: The small amplifier inside a condenser microphone that turns the capsule's extremely high impedance into a low-impedance output that can drive a cable. It needs power.
example: Without its impedance converter, a condenser capsule's signal would be lost in a few metres of cable.

definition: A transformer with more turns on its output than its input, raising voltage (and impedance). Passive ribbon mics use one to boost the ribbon's tiny output.
example: A 1:30 step-up transformer raises a ribbon's microvolts to millivolts.

definition: A plot of a microphone's (or speaker's) sensitivity in each direction. Common microphone patterns are omnidirectional, cardioid, supercardioid, hypercardioid and figure-8. Directions where response falls to zero are called nulls.
example: A cardioid's polar pattern is heart-shaped, with a null directly behind.

definition: Picking up (or radiating) sound equally from all directions. A pressure microphone, sealed behind its diaphragm, is naturally omnidirectional and has no proximity effect.
example: An omni measurement mic responds the same whichever way it points.

definition: A microphone pattern equally sensitive front and back (opposite polarity) with nulls at the sides. Ribbon and pressure-gradient mics are naturally figure-8.
example: A figure-8 mic placed between two singers picks up both and rejects the sides.

definition: A heart-shaped microphone pattern: full sensitivity at the front, about −6 dB at the sides and a null at the rear (180°). It is the most common pattern for vocal mics.
example: Put a stage wedge directly behind a cardioid vocal mic.

definition: A first-order pattern narrower than cardioid (about −8.7 dB at the sides) with nulls near 125° and a small rear lobe.
example: Place wedges at about 125° off-axis for a supercardioid.

definition: A first-order pattern narrower still (−12 dB at the sides) with nulls near 110° and a rear lobe only 6 dB down.
example: A hypercardioid rejects side spill better than a cardioid but picks up more from directly behind.

definition: The smaller region of sensitivity at the back of a supercardioid or hypercardioid microphone.
example: A hypercardioid's rear lobe is only about 6 dB down, so a wedge directly behind it can feed back.

definition: A microphone whose diaphragm is open to sound only at the front, so it responds to pressure, which has no direction. It is omnidirectional.
example: Measurement microphones are pressure microphones.

definition: A microphone open at front and back that responds to the difference in pressure between the two sides. It is directional and shows proximity effect.
example: A ribbon mic is a pressure-gradient microphone.

definition: Any polar pattern that is a mix of omni and figure-8, described by r(θ) = A + (1 − A)·cos θ. Cardioid, supercardioid and hypercardioid are first-order.
example: A = 0.5 gives a cardioid.

definition: A trigonometric function of an angle: 1 at 0°, 0 at 90° and −1 at 180°. It describes the figure-8 part of microphone polar patterns.
example: cos 90° = 0, which is why a figure-8 mic has a null at the side.

definition: The Greek letter theta, commonly used for an angle. In microphone patterns it is the angle of the sound source away from the front axis.
example: θ = 180° means the source is directly behind the mic.

definition: A bass boost in directional (pressure-gradient) microphones when the source is very close, growing as the distance shrinks. Omnidirectional pressure mics have none.
example: A singer "eating" a cardioid mic gets a warmer, boomier sound.

definition: A switch on a microphone or channel that applies a high-pass filter, reducing low frequencies to counter proximity effect, rumble or handling noise.
example: Engaging a mic's 80 Hz bass-cut removes stage rumble.

definition: A microphone's output voltage for a given sound pressure, normally at 1 kHz and 1 Pa (94 dB SPL). Quoted in millivolts per pascal (mV/Pa) or decibels relative to 1 V per pascal (dBV/Pa).
example: The SM58 gives about 1.85 mV/Pa (−54.5 dBV/Pa); a U 87 Ai about 28 mV/Pa.

definition: The noise a microphone's own electronics produce, quoted as the SPL that would give the same output, usually A-weighted. Lower is quieter.
example: The U 87 Ai's self-noise is 12 dB-A: very quiet.

definition: An amplifier's noise expressed as the voltage that would produce it at the input, so it can be compared directly with the signal. For mic preamps, measured with a 150 Ω source over 20 Hz–20 kHz, good figures are around −125 to −130 dBu; about −131 dBu is the thermal-noise limit of the source resistance itself.
example: A low-output dynamic mic needs a preamp with low EIN.

definition: Random noise generated by the motion of electrons in any resistance. It sets a floor even for passive dynamic and ribbon mics.
example: A 150 Ω mic coil generates thermal noise of roughly −131 dBu over 20 kHz.

definition: The highest sound pressure level a microphone can handle before its distortion reaches a stated figure, often 0.5% or 1% THD.
example: Neumann quotes 117 dB SPL max for the U 87 Ai (127 dB with the pad).

definition: A switchable fixed attenuator (often 10 or 20 dB) that lowers a signal so a loud source does not overload a microphone or preamp.
example: Use the DI box's pad if a synth's line output overloads the mic input.

definition: The combined level of the harmonics a device adds to a pure tone, as a percentage of the output (or in dB). Lower is cleaner.
example: A good power amp may manage 0.01% THD; power ratings at 10% THD are heavily distorted.

definition: DC power sent to a microphone along the same balanced cable that carries its signal, applied equally to both signal wires. P48 (+48 V) is the standard version.
example: Condenser mics and active DI boxes run on phantom power from the mixer.

definition: The IEC 61938 phantom-power standard: +48 V fed through two matched 6.81 kΩ resistors to pins 2 and 3 of an XLR, returning via pin 1, up to 10 mA per mic. P12 and P24 are lower-voltage variants.
example: A mic drawing 10 mA sees only about 14 V at its connector on P48.

definition: The IEC standard that defines microphone phantom-powering systems, including P48, P24 and P12.
example: IEC 61938 sets the 6.81 kΩ feed resistors for P48.

definition: The standard three-pin locking connector for microphones and balanced audio. Pin 1 is shield/ground, pin 2 is hot (+) and pin 3 cold (−).
example: Phantom power appears on pins 2 and 3 of an XLR.

definition: A connection using two signal wires with matched impedances to ground, so interference picked up equally on both is cancelled at a differential input.
example: A balanced mic cable can run 50 m on stage with little hum.

definition: A voltage that appears equally on both wires of a balanced pair. A differential input rejects it; that is how balanced lines cancel interference and why phantom power does not reach an ideal floating mic coil.
example: Hum induced equally in both wires is common-mode and is cancelled.

definition: Using series capacitors (or transformers) to stop a steady DC voltage while passing the audio signal. Preamps use it to keep phantom voltage out of their circuitry.
example: Phantom-capable preamp inputs have DC-blocking capacitors rated above 48 V.

definition: Connecting or disconnecting equipment while it is powered. With phantom on, the XLR pins do not connect at the same instant, which can send a damaging pulse.
example: Turn phantom off before hot-plugging a ribbon mic.

definition: An amplifier that raises a microphone's millivolt-level signal by tens of decibels to line level. Its gain control (trim) is the first and most important gain stage.
example: An SM58 on a singer needs about 46 dB of preamp gain to reach +4 dBu.

definition: A rule of thumb for multiple mics: the distance between mics should be at least three times each mic's distance from its source, keeping leakage about 9.5 dB down so comb filtering stays mild.
example: Mics 30 cm from their singers should be at least 90 cm apart.

definition: Sound from one source picked up by a microphone meant for another.
example: The hi-hat leaking into the snare mic is spill.

definition: A classic, rugged dynamic cardioid vocal microphone made by Shure since 1966, often used as a reference stage mic. Shure quotes −54.5 dBV/Pa sensitivity.
example: An SM58 survives being dropped on stage and still works.

definition: A widely used large-diaphragm studio condenser microphone by Neumann, switchable between omni, cardioid and figure-8. Neumann quotes 28 mV/Pa and 12 dB-A self-noise in cardioid.
example: Many vocal recordings use a U 87 Ai.

definition: One thousandth of a volt. Microphone outputs are typically a few millivolts to tens of millivolts.
example: A dynamic mic might give 2 mV at 94 dB SPL.

definition: One thousandth of an ampere. Phantom-powered microphones draw a few milliamps.
example: P48 allows up to 10 mA per microphone.

definition: One thousand ohms.
example: P48 feed resistors are 6.81 kΩ.

definition: Sound that travels straight from source to listener or mic without reflecting. Its balance with room reflections changes with distance.
example: Moving a mic closer increases direct sound relative to the room.

definition: A device that turns an electrical signal into sound. A loudspeaker system is one or more drivers plus an enclosure and usually a crossover.
example: A two-way bookshelf loudspeaker has a woofer, a tweeter and a passive crossover in one box.

definition: The motor and diaphragm that actually move air in a loudspeaker; a single cone or dome unit. Nearly all are moving-coil (electrodynamic) drivers.
example: A 2-way speaker contains two drivers: a woofer and a tweeter.

definition: A design in which a coil of wire attached to a diaphragm sits in a magnetic field. Current in the coil moves it (a speaker), or moving it generates a voltage (a dynamic microphone).
example: Almost every speaker you will meet is moving-coil.

definition: The coil of fine wire wound on a light former, attached to a driver's cone and sitting in the magnet's gap. Current through it produces the force that moves the cone.
example: Too much average power overheats the voice coil and can burn it out.

definition: The narrow ring-shaped space in a driver's motor where steel pole pieces concentrate the permanent magnet's field and the voice coil sits.
example: A strong field in the gap means more force per amp of current.

definition: Neodymium (NdFeB) magnets are very strong for their size and weight; ferrite (ceramic) magnets are cheaper and heavier. Both are used in driver motors.
example: A neodymium motor can make a large PA woofer several kilograms lighter than the ferrite equivalent.

definition: The diaphragm of a woofer or midrange driver that pushes the air. It must be light and stiff; paper, polypropylene, aluminium and composites are common.
example: An aluminium cone is stiff, pushing breakup higher, but rings sharply when it breaks up.

definition: The flexible ring joining the outer edge of a driver's cone to the basket. With the spider it centres the cone and provides a restoring force.
example: Old foam surrounds can rot and need replacing.

definition: The corrugated fabric disc behind a driver's cone that keeps the voice coil centred in the gap and helps pull the cone back to rest.
example: The spider and surround together form the suspension.

definition: The surround and spider of a driver: they hold the cone in place and act as a spring that pulls it back to rest.
example: A stiffer suspension raises the driver's resonance.

definition: The metal or plastic chassis that holds a driver's magnet, suspension and cone together and bolts to the baffle.
example: A cast-aluminium basket is stiffer than pressed steel.

definition: The product of the magnetic flux density in the gap (B) and the length of voice-coil wire in it (l), in tesla-metres (T·m). Force on the coil = Bl × current.
example: A driver with Bl = 7 T·m feels 7 N per amp.

definition: The SI unit of magnetic flux density. A driver's magnet gap typically has around 1 T; Bl is quoted in tesla-metres (T·m).
example: A gap of 1 T with 7 m of wire in it gives Bl = 7 T·m.

definition: The SI unit of force: the force that accelerates 1 kg by 1 m/s².
example: A voice coil with Bl = 7 T·m and 1 A feels a force of 7 N.

definition: How concentrated a magnetic field is, measured in tesla (T). Higher flux density in a driver's gap gives more force for the same current.
example: Neodymium motors can reach well over 1 T in the gap.

definition: The total mass that moves in a driver: cone, voice coil, part of the suspension and the air load. With the suspension compliance it sets the resonance.
example: Adding mass to a cone lowers its Fs.

definition: How springy a driver's suspension is: the inverse of its stiffness, in metres per newton (m/N). Higher compliance means a softer suspension.
example: A compliance of 1 mm/N means 1 N of force moves the cone 1 mm.

definition: The effective radiating area of a driver's cone, in square metres, including about half the surround. It is a Thiele–Small parameter.
example: An 8-inch woofer has Sd of roughly 0.02 m².

definition: The frequency at which a driver's moving mass bounces on its suspension spring when it is not in a box. Below it the output falls away. It is a Thiele–Small parameter, usually written Fs.
example: A typical 8-inch woofer has Fs around 30–50 Hz.

definition: The tendency of a system (a mass on a spring, an air cavity, a room) to vibrate strongly at a particular frequency. A synth filter's resonance control works the same way, boosting a narrow band around the cut-off.
example: A ported box's air resonates at its tuning frequency.

definition: The voltage generated by a moving voice coil in its magnet, which opposes the driving current. It is why a driver's impedance peaks at resonance.
example: At Fs the cone moves most, so back-EMF is largest and the impedance peaks.

definition: The total opposition a circuit offers to alternating current, in ohms (Ω). Unlike resistance, it can vary with frequency and include a phase shift between voltage and current.
example: A speaker labelled 8 Ω may measure 6.7 Ω at 600 Hz and 40 Ω at its resonance.

definition: A single rounded impedance label (4, 8 or 16 Ω) for a speaker. IEC 60268-5 expects the minimum in the rated frequency range not to fall below 80% of it.
example: An 8 Ω speaker should not dip below 6.4 Ω in its operating range.

definition: A plot of a speaker's impedance magnitude against frequency, showing the resonance peak(s) and the inductive rise.
example: A ported box's impedance curve has two peaks with a dip at the tuning frequency.

definition: The plain DC resistance of a driver's voice coil, in ohms. It is typically about 5–7 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver.
example: Measure Re with a multimeter across the driver terminals.

definition: The inductance of a driver's voice coil, in henries (usually fractions of a millihenry). It makes impedance rise at high frequencies.
example: Le = 0.48 mH adds about 30 Ω of reactance at 10 kHz.

definition: The IEC standard for loudspeaker measurements and ratings, including the rule that minimum impedance should not fall below 80% of the nominal value.
example: IEC 60268-5 defines how rated impedance should be stated.

definition: The SPL a speaker produces on-axis at 1 m for a reference input: 1 W into its nominal impedance, or 2.83 V. Higher sensitivity needs less amplifier power for the same level.
example: An 87 dB/1 W/1 m speaker gives 97 dB SPL at 1 m with 10 W.

definition: The fraction of electrical power a speaker converts into acoustic power. For a typical home speaker it is only about 1%; the rest becomes heat.
example: Horn-loaded PA speakers are several times more efficient than hi-fi boxes.

definition: The loss of output at high power as a voice coil heats up and its resistance rises, so the speaker gets less loud than the power increase predicts.
example: After an hour at high level a woofer may play 3 dB quieter than calculated.

definition: How a device's output level (and phase) varies with frequency for a fixed input. Often summarised by ±3 dB limits.
example: A monitor's frequency response might be 45 Hz–20 kHz ±3 dB.

definition: On-axis means directly in front of a speaker or microphone along its main axis; off-axis means at an angle to it. Off-axis response usually loses treble.
example: Off-axis curves at 30° and 60° show how a speaker beams.

definition: How widely a speaker spreads sound across angles. Wide dispersion covers more listeners; controlled dispersion keeps sound off walls.
example: A horn may give 90° × 40° dispersion.

definition: How much a source or microphone favours some directions over others. Speakers become more directional as wavelength shrinks compared with their size.
example: A woofer is nearly omnidirectional at 100 Hz but directional at 2 kHz.

definition: The narrowing of a driver's dispersion at frequencies where the wavelength becomes comparable with the cone size, roughly above f = c/(2πa) for a piston of radius a.
example: A 13 cm woofer starts beaming around 840 Hz.

definition: A model of a speaker cone as a perfectly rigid disc moving back and forth as one piece. Real cones behave like this only at lower frequencies.
example: Below breakup, a woofer cone acts as a piston.

definition: k is the wavenumber (2π divided by the wavelength) and a the radius of the source. When ka is about 1, the source starts becoming directional.
example: At ka = 1, the circumference of the cone equals one wavelength.

definition: A driver's maximum excursion (one-way cone travel) under a stated criterion, often where the coil starts leaving the gap or distortion reaches a set level. Definitions vary between manufacturers.
example: A woofer with Xmax = 5 mm can move about 5 mm each way before its stated distortion or geometry limit is reached.

definition: How far a driver's cone moves from rest. Bass needs large excursion; too much causes distortion or physical damage.
example: Below a ported box's tuning, excursion rises steeply.

definition: How much power a speaker or driver can take. It has a thermal limit (coil heating from average power) and a mechanical (excursion) limit.
example: A "100 W" speaker rating describes a specific test, not a safe power for every signal.

definition: A driver designed for low (bass) frequencies, typically 13–38 cm across, often also handling the mids in a two-way speaker.
example: A 6.5-inch woofer covers 40 Hz to 2.5 kHz in many bookshelf speakers.

definition: A speaker for the lowest frequencies, usually below about 80–120 Hz, with a large long-excursion driver.
example: A PA often has subwoofers on the floor below the main speakers.

definition: A driver for the middle frequencies, roughly 300 Hz to 3 kHz, covering the vocal region in a three-way speaker.
example: A three-way speaker has a woofer, a midrange and a tweeter.

definition: A small driver, often a 19–28 mm dome, for high frequencies, typically above about 2–3 kHz. It is easily damaged by too much low-frequency energy.
example: Clipping an amplifier can burn out a tweeter.

definition: A speaker that splits the band between two (or more) drivers using a crossover, each driver covering the range it handles best.
example: A two-way monitor crosses from woofer to tweeter around 2–3 kHz.

definition: A high-efficiency driver whose diaphragm pressurises a small chamber that feeds a narrow throat and horn through a phase plug. Used for mids and highs in PA speakers.
example: A PA top box may use a 1.4-inch compression driver on a horn.

definition: A shaped insert in front of a compression driver's diaphragm whose channels equalise the path lengths from different parts of the diaphragm to the throat, so their sound arrives in step.
example: Without a phase plug, path differences would cause high-frequency cancellation.

definition: A flared duct in front of a driver. Its narrow throat and widening mouth match the diaphragm to the air, greatly improving efficiency, and its shape controls dispersion.
example: Horn-loaded PA speakers can reach about 110 dB SPL at 2.83 V/1 m.

definition: When a cone stops moving as a rigid piston and bending waves travel across it, causing response peaks, changed dispersion and sometimes coloration.
example: Metal-cone woofers often have a sharp breakup peak around 5–8 kHz.

definition: The margin between normal operating level and the level where a device clips or is damaged. Headroom absorbs peaks that are much louder than the average.
example: Peaking at −18 dBFS leaves 18 dB of headroom before digital clipping.

definition: At low frequencies, the rear wave of a bare driver diffracts round the edge and cancels the front wave, so almost no bass is radiated.
example: Hold a bare woofer in the air and the bass vanishes: an acoustic short circuit.

definition: A source radiating equal and opposite pressure from its front and back, with nulls at the sides. A bare driver or an open-baffle speaker is a dipole.
example: An open-baffle speaker has a figure-8 radiation pattern because it is a dipole.

definition: A source radiating equally in all directions, like a pulsating sphere. A sealed box at low frequencies behaves like one.
example: A sealed subwoofer is nearly a monopole at 40 Hz.

definition: The board a driver is mounted in. It separates the front and rear waves and its size sets where baffle step happens.
example: A wider baffle moves the baffle step to a lower frequency.

definition: The box a driver is mounted in. It stops the rear wave cancelling the front, or redirects it to help, and largely sets the bass response.
example: A 20 L sealed enclosure gives a particular woofer a 60 Hz resonance.

definition: The drop of up to 6 dB in on-axis level as frequency falls and a speaker's radiation changes from half-space (in front of the baffle) to full space (wrapping round the cabinet). It happens where the wavelength is comparable with the baffle width.
example: A 20 cm-wide bookshelf speaker has its baffle step around a few hundred hertz.

definition: A gentle shelf, usually in the crossover, that lowers everything above the baffle step so the overall response stays balanced.
example: A speaker designed for wall placement may need less baffle step compensation.

definition: An enclosure that traps the rear wave completely. The air inside acts as an extra spring, raising the resonance; below it, output falls at 12 dB per octave.
example: A 20 L sealed box with the right driver gives a smooth Butterworth roll-off.

definition: An enclosure with a port (tube) whose air mass resonates with the box air as a Helmholtz resonator, reinforcing bass near the tuning frequency. Below tuning, output falls at 24 dB per octave and the cone is uncontrolled.
example: Most powered studio monitors are ported.

definition: The tube or slot in a ported enclosure through which the box air moves. The air plug in it acts as a mass bouncing on the springy box air.
example: A 5 cm × 15 cm port in a 30 L box tunes to about 32 Hz.

definition: The Helmholtz resonance frequency of a ported box (Fb), where the port radiates most strongly and the cone moves least. For a sealed box the equivalent is the system resonance, Fc.
example: Below Fb the woofer is effectively in free air and can over-excurse.

definition: A cavity of air connected to the outside by a neck: the air in the neck acts as a mass and the cavity air as a spring, so it resonates at one frequency. Blowing across a bottle is the classic example.
example: A ported speaker box and some bass traps are Helmholtz resonators.

definition: Noise from turbulent air in a port when the air speed is too high, usually because the port is too narrow for the output.
example: Flaring the port ends reduces chuffing.

definition: A high-pass filter below the audible bass range, used in ported systems to stop very low frequencies over-excursing the driver below the box tuning.
example: A 25 Hz subsonic filter protects a sub tuned to 30 Hz.

definition: A speaker with drivers on a flat panel and no box, so it stays a dipole. Front-to-back cancellation adds about 6 dB per octave of extra bass loss.
example: Open-baffle speakers need lots of excursion or EQ for deep bass.

definition: An enclosure where the driver's rear wave travels down a long, folded, damped duct, typically a quarter wavelength at a target low frequency, before leaving through a vent to reinforce the bass.
example: A line of about 2.1 m is a quarter wavelength at 40 Hz.

definition: One quarter of a wavelength. A reflection from a wall a quarter wavelength away travels an extra half wavelength and returns out of phase; a porous absorber works best where air velocity peaks, a quarter wavelength from a hard wall.
example: A quarter wavelength at 100 Hz is about 0.86 m.

definition: A set of small-signal driver parameters (Fs, Qts, Qes, Qms, Vas, Re, Le, Bl, Sd and others), measured at low levels, that let designers predict a driver's bass response in a box. Named after Neville Thiele (1961) and Richard Small (1972–73).
example: Box-modelling software needs Fs, Qts and Vas at minimum.

definition: A measure of how sharply a resonance peaks, or how lightly damped it is. High Q means a tall, narrow, ringing peak; low Q a broad, well-damped one.
example: A sealed box with Q = 1.1 has a hump before rolling off.

definition: A driver's total Q at its free-air resonance: how damped that resonance is, combining Qms and Qes as Qts = Qms × Qes / (Qms + Qes). Most drivers fall between about 0.2 and 0.5.
example: A driver with Qts = 0.35 suits a sealed box of moderate size.

definition: A driver's electrical Q at resonance: the damping provided by the motor (back-EMF through the amplifier and voice-coil resistance).
example: A strong motor gives a low Qes.

definition: A driver's mechanical Q at resonance: the damping from losses in the suspension alone. Usually several times larger than Qes.
example: Qms = 4 with Qes = 0.4 gives Qts ≈ 0.36.

definition: The volume of air with the same springiness (compliance) as a driver's suspension, usually in litres. It depends on both suspension stiffness and cone area.
example: Putting a driver with Vas = 60 L in a 20 L box makes the box air three times stiffer than its suspension.

definition: A rough guide to box type: EBP = Fs / Qes. Around 50 suggests a sealed box; around 100 a ported one. A starting point, not a design method.
example: Fs = 30 Hz and Qes = 0.5 give EBP = 60.

definition: In sealed-box design, α = Vas / Vb: how stiff the box air is compared with the driver's suspension. It sets how far the box raises the resonance and Q.
example: Vas = 60 L in a 20 L box gives α = 3, so Fc = 2 × Fs.

definition: The internal air volume of a speaker enclosure, usually in litres, written Vb.
example: A bookshelf speaker might have Vb around 10–15 L.

aliases: system Q of a sealed box
definition: The total Q of a driver in a sealed box, Qtc = Qts × √(1 + α). It sets the shape of the bass roll-off: 0.5 is critically damped, 0.707 maximally flat (Butterworth), above about 1 peaky.
example: Qtc = 0.707 gives −3 dB at the box resonance.

definition: The resonance frequency of a driver mounted in a sealed box, Fc = Fs × √(1 + α), higher than its free-air resonance because the box air adds stiffness.
example: A 30 Hz driver in a 20 L box might have Fc = 60 Hz.

definition: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original: √9 = 3. Resonance frequencies scale with the square root of stiffness.
example: Quadrupling the stiffness doubles the resonance frequency, because √4 = 2.

definition: An extra length added to a port's physical length because the air just outside each open end also moves with it. Roughly 0.6–0.85 times the port radius per end, depending on flanging.
example: A 15 cm port of 2.5 cm radius behaves like about 18.7 cm.

definition: A unit of volume: 1 litre = 0.001 cubic metres (m³). Speaker box volumes and Vas are usually given in litres.
example: A 30 L box is 0.03 m³.

definition: The SI unit of volume: a cube 1 m on each side, equal to 1000 litres.
example: A 5 × 3.6 × 2.4 m room is 43.2 m³.

definition: The SI unit of area. Room surface areas and port cross-sections are measured in square metres.
example: A 1 m × 1 m absorber panel covers 1 m².

definition: A particular combination of driver parameters, box volume and tuning that gives a chosen bass filter shape, such as Butterworth or Chebyshev, borrowed from electrical filter theory.
example: A Qtc of 0.707 sealed box is a Butterworth alignment.

definition: A filter design whose passband is as flat as possible ("maximally flat"), −3 dB at its corner frequency. Introduced by Stephen Butterworth in 1930.
example: A second-order Butterworth high-pass has Q = 0.707.

definition: A filter design that trades some ripple in the passband for a steeper roll-off or more extension. Named after the mathematician Pafnuty Chebyshev.
example: A Chebyshev box alignment gives a small bass hump but goes lower.

definition: Damped exactly enough that a system returns to rest as fast as possible without overshooting. For a second-order system this is Q = 0.5.
example: A sealed box with Qtc = 0.5 is critically damped and −6 dB at Fc.

definition: The number of reactive stages (poles) in a filter. For conventional filters each order adds about 6 dB per octave of asymptotic slope and 90° of total phase rotation.
example: A fourth-order filter falls at 24 dB per octave.

definition: How steeply a filter's level falls: the number of decibels lost for each halving (or doubling) of frequency beyond the corner.
example: A 12 dB/octave high-pass at 60 Hz is 12 dB down at 30 Hz.

definition: The gradual reduction of level beyond a filter's or speaker's corner frequency, described in dB per octave.
example: A sealed box rolls off at 12 dB/octave below Fc.

definition: A filter that passes frequencies above its corner and reduces those below. On a mixer channel it removes rumble; a speaker in a box is acoustically a high-pass filter.
example: An 80 Hz HPF on a vocal channel cuts stage rumble.

definition: Vibration of an enclosure's walls at their natural frequencies, making the box itself radiate sound that colours the output.
example: Knock on a thin MDF panel and you hear its resonance.

definition: Internal struts or shelves that stiffen enclosure panels, pushing their resonances higher and reducing their amplitude.
example: A window brace across the middle of a tall cabinet stiffens both side panels.

definition: Absorbent fill or lining inside a speaker box that reduces internal standing waves and can make a sealed box behave as if somewhat larger.
example: Polyester wadding in a sealed box can raise its apparent volume by up to about 15%.

definition: Anything that removes energy from a vibrating system so its oscillations die away faster and its resonant peak is lower.
example: A well-damped woofer stops moving quickly when the note ends.

definition: Medium-density fibreboard: an engineered board of wood fibres and resin, dense, flat and cheap, widely used for speaker cabinets. Its dust is a respiratory hazard when cut.
example: Most DIY speaker boxes are 18 mm MDF.

definition: A wave pattern that stays in place, formed when a wave and its reflection overlap at a frequency where they reinforce. It has fixed points of maximum and minimum pressure.
example: Two parallel walls 5 m apart set up a standing wave at 34.3 Hz.

definition: Measured or valid at low levels where a device behaves linearly. Thiele–Small parameters are small-signal values.
example: At high excursion, Bl and compliance change, so small-signal parameters no longer hold.

definition: A driver-like cone with no motor, used instead of a port: the box air drives it to reinforce bass like a port, without port noise.
example: Small Bluetooth speakers often use passive radiators.

definition: Programs that simulate a driver in an enclosure from its Thiele–Small parameters, predicting response, excursion and port air speed.
example: WinISD and VituixCAD are examples used by DIY builders.

definition: A set of filters that splits an audio signal into frequency bands so each driver in a multi-way speaker gets only the frequencies it handles well. The outputs must add back together smoothly in the air.
example: A two-way crossover at 2.5 kHz sends bass and mids to the woofer and treble to the tweeter.

definition: The frequency at which a crossover hands over from one driver to the next, where both contribute; written fc.
example: An LR4 crossover is −6 dB per side at fc.

definition: A crossover built from inductors, capacitors and resistors between one power amplifier and the drivers. It carries speaker-level current and its behaviour depends on the drivers' impedance.
example: Most hi-fi speakers have a passive crossover inside the box.

definition: A crossover that filters at line level using op-amp circuits, before a separate power amplifier for each driver.
example: An active crossover means a clipping woofer amp cannot send distortion to the tweeter.

definition: An active crossover implemented in digital signal processing, often with per-driver delay, EQ and limiting. Used in most powered monitors and PA processors.
example: A DSP crossover can delay the tweeter by 0.2 ms to align it with the woofer.

definition: Digital signal processing: manipulating audio as numbers in software or a dedicated chip, for filtering, EQ, delay, dynamics and more.
example: A PA processor uses DSP for crossover filters and limiters.

definition: A filter built from inductors (L) and capacitors (C). Passive speaker crossovers and class D output filters are LC filters.
example: A second-order LC low-pass falls at 12 dB/octave.

definition: A circuit of a resistor (R) and a capacitor (C), the simplest first-order filter or timing network.
example: A Zobel network is a series RC across a woofer.

definition: The steady slope a filter's response approaches far from its corner frequency, such as 24 dB per octave for a fourth-order filter.
example: Near the corner the slope is gentler than its asymptotic value.

definition: A filter's passband is the range of frequencies it lets through; its stopband is the range it attenuates.
example: A tweeter's high-pass filter has its stopband below the crossover.

definition: A filter whose transfer function has no zeros (except at infinity), such as Butterworth or Chebyshev low-passes. Its order sets its asymptotic slope.
example: A Butterworth low-pass is an all-pole filter.

definition: Where a wave is in its cycle, measured in degrees (360° per cycle). Filters and delays shift phase, which decides whether two signals reinforce or cancel when added.
example: A 1 ms delay is a 360° phase shift at 1 kHz.

definition: Which way round a signal is: reversing polarity flips the waveform upside down (positive becomes negative) at all frequencies. Swapping a driver's + and − wires reverses its polarity.
example: A second-order Butterworth crossover needs the tweeter wired in reverse polarity.

definition: A crossover made by cascading two Butterworth filters of the same order on each side, so each output is −6 dB at the crossover and they sum flat. Published by Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley in 1976.
example: LR4 is the common choice in PA processors.

definition: A fourth-order Linkwitz–Riley crossover (two second-order Butterworths per side): 24 dB per octave, outputs in phase at all frequencies, summing flat as an all-pass.
example: An LR4 crossover at 100 Hz is common between subs and tops.

definition: A second-order Linkwitz–Riley crossover (two first-order sections per side): 12 dB per octave, outputs 180° apart, so one driver is reversed in polarity to sum flat.
example: LR2 needs one driver wired in reverse polarity.

definition: An eighth-order Linkwitz–Riley crossover: 48 dB per octave, practical mainly in DSP.
example: An LR8 sub low-pass is about 48 dB down one octave above the crossover, against about 24 dB for an LR4.

definition: Short for a second-order Butterworth filter: 12 dB per octave, −3 dB at its corner. Used as a crossover, its outputs sum with a +3 dB peak (one driver inverted) or a notch.
example: An LR4 is two BW2 filters in series on each side.

definition: Short for low-pass: the filter output that passes frequencies below the crossover, feeding the woofer.
example: At the LR4 crossover, LP is at −6 dB.

definition: Short for high-pass: the filter output that passes frequencies above the crossover, feeding the tweeter.
example: At the LR4 crossover, HP is at −6 dB.

definition: A filter that passes all frequencies at the same level but changes their phase. The summed output of an LR4 crossover behaves as an all-pass.
example: An all-pass filter can be used to correct phase without changing the frequency response.

definition: In filter maths, s is a complex frequency variable; on the frequency axis s = jω (or j × f/fc in normalised form). Filter responses are written as fractions in s.
example: A first-order low-pass is 1/(1 + s).

definition: The number j (i in maths) whose square is −1. Engineers use it to represent phase: impedances and filter responses are complex numbers with a real and an imaginary (j) part.
example: An inductor's impedance is j × 2π × f × L.

definition: Frequency expressed as a ratio to a reference such as the crossover frequency, so that fc = 1. It lets one formula describe a filter at any corner frequency.
example: At twice the crossover, the normalised frequency is 2.

definition: A formula describing how a filter or system changes each input frequency's level and phase.
example: The transfer function 1/(1 + s) describes a first-order low-pass.

definition: The point from which a driver's sound effectively appears to radiate. On a flat baffle a woofer's acoustic centre is usually further back than a tweeter's, creating a time offset.
example: An 8 cm acoustic-centre offset is about 233 µs at 343 m/s.

definition: Delaying one driver (or speaker) so that sound from all arrives at the listener at the same time, keeping the crossover summation correct.
example: A DSP delay of 0.23 ms on the tweeter can align it with a recessed woofer.

definition: A front baffle with a step or a backward slope that physically lines up the acoustic centres of the drivers.
example: Some studio monitors use a sloped baffle instead of DSP delay.

definition: The way the combined response of two drivers varies with vertical angle, because moving up or down changes their path lengths. The direction of strongest output is the main lobe.
example: Standing up in front of a two-way speaker can put you in a lobing dip at the crossover.

definition: A filter whose phase response changes linearly with frequency, giving constant group delay over the frequency range where that phase is defined. It avoids frequency-dependent timing dispersion there, but changing the magnitudes of frequency components can still change the waveform. Symmetric FIR filters are a common digital implementation; latency depends on the design.
example: A symmetric three-tap moving-average FIR has one sample of delay, while reducing some frequencies more than others; its output need not have the input waveform’s shape.

definition: A finite impulse response filter: a digital filter whose output is a weighted sum of a finite number of past inputs. It can be linear-phase, at the cost of latency.
example: Large PA processors offer FIR filters for phase correction.

definition: A coil of wire that opposes changes in current. Its impedance rises with frequency, so in series with a woofer it acts as a low-pass filter. Measured in henries (H).
example: A 0.42 mH inductor in series with an 8 Ω woofer gives a 3 kHz first-order low-pass.

definition: The SI unit of inductance. Crossover inductors are usually fractions of a millihenry (mH) to a few millihenries.
The SI unit of capacitance. Crossover capacitors are usually a few microfarads (µF, millionths of a farad).
A component storing charge between two plates. Its impedance falls as frequency rises, so in series with a tweeter it acts as a high-pass filter. Measured in farads (F).
example: A 6.6 µF capacitor in series with an 8 Ω tweeter gives a 3 kHz first-order high-pass.

definition: A pair of resistors used as an attenuator in a passive crossover to lower a more sensitive tweeter's level while keeping the load the crossover sees roughly constant.
example: An L-pad can drop a tweeter by 4 dB to match the woofer.

definition: In loudspeakers, a series resistor and capacitor placed across a driver to cancel the rise in impedance caused by voice-coil inductance, so a passive crossover sees a more constant load.
example: A Zobel network across a woofer flattens its impedance above 1 kHz.

definition: An operational amplifier: a high-gain integrated-circuit amplifier used with a few resistors and capacitors to build filters, buffers and gain stages.
example: An active crossover is often built from op-amp filter stages.

definition: The standard signal level between audio equipment: about +4 dBu (1.23 V RMS) for professional gear and −10 dBV (0.32 V RMS) for consumer gear.
example: A synth's output is line level and needs a DI or line input, not a mic input with phantom on.

definition: The high-voltage, high-current signal from a power amplifier's output that drives loudspeakers, typically tens of volts and several amps.
example: Passive crossovers operate at speaker level.

definition: The very low signal level from a microphone, typically a few millivolts, which needs a preamp to reach line level.
example: A DI box converts a line-level synth to mic level.

definition: An amplifier that delivers enough voltage and current to drive loudspeakers: a voltage amplifier with very low output impedance. The speaker's impedance decides how much power it draws.
example: A 26 dB power amp turns +4 dBu into about 24.5 V RMS: 75 W into 8 Ω.

definition: How much an amplifier multiplies its input voltage, as a ratio or in decibels (20 × log10 of the ratio).
example: 26 dB of voltage gain is a factor of 20.

definition: The input voltage that drives a power amplifier to its full rated output. A lower figure means more gain.
example: An amp with 1.4 V input sensitivity reaches 100 W into 8 Ω from a 1.4 V input.

definition: A way of averaging an alternating signal that gives the steady DC value with the same heating power. For a sine wave, RMS = peak ÷ √2 ≈ 0.707 × peak.
example: A 28.3 V RMS sine has peaks of 40 V.

definition: A letter describing how an amplifier's output devices conduct over the signal cycle (A, B, AB, D, ...), a broad guide to its efficiency and linearity.
example: Most powered speakers today use class D amplifiers.

definition: An amplifier whose output devices conduct over the whole cycle, biased at high standing current. Very linear with no crossover distortion, but inefficient: ideally 25% or up to 50% depending on topology.
example: A stereo class A amp rated at 20 W per channel can draw around 100 W from the mains even when silent.

definition: A push-pull amplifier where each output device conducts exactly half the cycle. Theoretical maximum efficiency is π/4 ≈ 78.5%, but it suffers crossover distortion.
example: Class B is rare in hi-fi because of crossover distortion.

definition: A push-pull amplifier with a small bias current so both devices conduct briefly around the handover, removing most crossover distortion. Long the standard for linear hi-fi and PA amps.
example: A class AB amp runs warm at idle but far cooler than class A.

definition: An amplifier whose output devices act as switches, fully on or off, switching far above the audio band. Very efficient (over 80–90%), small and cool-running.
example: Most powered speakers and PA amps now use class D.

definition: An output stage with two devices: one handles the positive half of the waveform, the other the negative.
example: Class B and AB are push-pull designs.

definition: Distortion where one output device of a push-pull amplifier hands over to the other near zero volts, because neither conducts properly there. Not related to speaker crossovers.
example: Class AB bias largely removes crossover distortion.

definition: A steady current deliberately passed through an amplifier's output devices with no signal, setting where they operate.
example: Class A uses a large bias current; class AB a small one.

definition: Encoding a signal in the width of fixed-frequency pulses. Class D amps use it (or similar schemes) so the averaged output follows the audio.
example: A class D amp might switch at 400 kHz with PWM.

definition: How often a class D amplifier's output switches, typically hundreds of kilohertz, far above audio. An output filter removes it.
example: A 400 kHz switching frequency is 20 times above the audio band.

definition: The LC filter after a class D amplifier's switches that removes the switching carrier, leaving the audio.
example: A class D output filter's response can change with the speaker load.

definition: Metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor: a fast, efficient transistor used as the switch in class D amps and in many power supplies.
example: Good MOSFETs let class D amps exceed 90% efficiency.

definition: A semiconductor device that controls a large current with a small signal, used as an amplifier or switch. Power amps use them as output devices.
example: A class AB stage has two output transistors in push-pull.

definition: Electromagnetic interference: unwanted electrical noise radiated or conducted from a circuit. Class D switching causes EMI that must be filtered and shielded.
example: Long unshielded speaker leads on a filterless class D amp can radiate EMI.

definition: A vacuum-tube amplifying device, still used in guitar and some hi-fi amps. Valve amps run at hundreds of volts and need output transformers.
example: Never run a valve guitar amp without a speaker or load connected.

definition: The transformer in a valve amplifier that matches the valves' high impedance to a low-impedance speaker. Running without a load can damage it.
example: A valve amp's output transformer has 4, 8 and 16 Ω taps.

definition: The fixed positive and negative DC voltages that power an amplifier. The output cannot swing beyond them; trying to causes clipping.
example: An amp with ±40 V rails clips just under 40 V peak.

definition: A finned metal part that draws heat away from power devices. Inefficient amplifiers need large heatsinks.
example: A 100 W class A amp needs heatsinks for about 300 W of heat.

definition: The average power an amplifier can deliver continuously into a stated load, over a stated bandwidth, at a stated distortion. Often loosely called "RMS power". It is the meaningful power rating.
example: "100 W continuous into 8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, at 0.1% THD" is a complete rating.

definition: The highest instantaneous power. For a sine wave it is twice the average power, so a "200 W peak" amp may be a 100 W continuous amp.
example: A 100 W sine reaches 200 W at its peaks.

definition: Peak music power output: a marketing figure with no standard test method, so it cannot be converted to continuous power or used to compare products.
example: A "1000 W PMPO" computer speaker may manage a few watts continuous.

definition: The impedance an amplifier's output drives, normally the speaker. Lower load impedance draws more current; amps state a minimum load they can safely drive.
example: Two 8 Ω speakers in parallel make a 4 Ω load.

definition: Bridge-tied load: driving one speaker from two amplifier channels in opposite polarity, doubling the voltage swing. Each channel effectively sees half the load impedance.
example: Bridging into 4 Ω asks each channel to drive 2 Ω.

definition: The ratio of a speaker's nominal impedance to an amplifier's output impedance (DF = Z_load / Z_out). Above a few tens, cable and voice-coil resistance dominate, so very high figures make little difference.
example: An amp with 0.01 Ω output impedance has DF 800 into 8 Ω, but about 34 at the end of 10 m of thin cable.

definition: The internal impedance of a source, as seen by its load. A power or headphone amp should have a very low output impedance so the load does not change its output.
example: A 10 Ω headphone output will change the response of 32 Ω headphones.

definition: The two-conductor cable from amplifier to speaker. Its resistance adds to the amp's output impedance, so long runs need thicker cable.
example: 10 m of 1.5 mm² cable has about 0.22 Ω round-trip resistance.

definition: How strongly a material resists current, in ohm-metres (Ω·m); written ρ. Copper is about 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.
example: A wire's resistance = resistivity × length ÷ cross-section area.

definition: When a signal tries to exceed the maximum a device can output, its peaks are flattened. Clipping adds harsh harmonics; in a power amp it can overheat tweeters.
example: An amp with 40 V rails clips any waveform asking for more than about 40 V.

definition: A light on an amplifier, mixer or interface that shows when the signal is clipping or close to it.
example: If the amp's clip indicator flickers on every kick drum, turn down.

definition: A waveform that switches between two levels, spending equal time at each (a 50% duty cycle). It contains only odd harmonics, at 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental's amplitude.
example: A hard-clipped sine approaches a square wave.

definition: Components of a sound at odd whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency (3×, 5×, 7×...). Clipping creates them.
example: A clipped 1 kHz note puts odd harmonics at 3, 5 and 7 kHz into the tweeter.

definition: A small amplifier designed to drive headphones, which need far less power than speakers but vary from about 16 Ω to several hundred ohms. It should have low output impedance.
example: 10 mW needs 0.57 V into 32 Ω but 1.73 V into 300 Ω.

definition: The household AC electricity supply (230 V, 50 Hz in the UK). It can kill: never open mains-powered equipment.
example: A power amplifier's mains wiring and supply capacitors can be lethal.

definition: The SI unit of power: one joule per second. Amplifier output and speaker power ratings are in watts.
example: 28.3 V RMS into 8 Ω is about 100 W.

definition: The connected chain of microphones, DI boxes, mixer, processing, amplifiers and loudspeakers that brings sources to listeners at the right level and balance.
example: A pub gig's sound system might be a small mixer and two powered speakers.

definition: A public address system: the loudspeakers, amplifiers and processing that reproduce sound for an audience. In live music, "the PA" usually means the main speaker system.
example: A festival PA has line-array mains, subwoofers and delay towers.

definition: The level of background noise in a system or device with no signal. Signals must stay well above it.
example: A mic preamp's noise floor might be around −128 dBu EIN.

definition: A device that combines many inputs into a few outputs with independent level, tone, routing and effects control for each.
example: A 16-channel mixing console might feed main L/R, four monitor mixes and two effects.

definition: Digital audio workstation: software for recording, editing and mixing audio and MIDI, such as Ableton Live, Logic or Reaper. Its mixer copies the analogue console layout.
example: Ableton Live's mixer has sends, returns and groups like a console.

definition: One input channel's controls on a mixer, usually in order: preamp gain, high-pass filter, insert, EQ, dynamics, aux sends, pan, fader and routing.
example: Each microphone gets its own channel strip.

definition: The control at the top of a channel strip that sets how much the preamp amplifies the incoming signal. It sets the channel's signal-to-noise ratio and headroom.
example: Set the trim with the singer at full voice.

definition: A send-and-return connection that loops a channel's signal out to an external processor and back, in series with the channel.
example: Patch a hardware compressor into the vocal channel's insert point.

definition: Adjusting the level of particular frequency ranges with filters (shelving, parametric, graphic) to shape tone, fix problems or make room for other sources.
example: Cutting 300 Hz on a muddy guitar is EQ.

definition: An EQ that boosts or cuts everything above (high shelf) or below (low shelf) a corner frequency by a set amount.
example: A −3 dB high shelf at 2 kHz is a baffle-step-style correction.

definition: An EQ band whose centre frequency, gain and bandwidth (Q) can all be set, for precise boosts or cuts.
example: A narrow parametric cut at 2.5 kHz removes a feedback ring.

definition: Processing that changes level according to the signal's own level: compressors, limiters, gates and expanders.
example: Many digital desks have a gate and compressor on every channel.

definition: A dynamics processor that reduces the level of a signal above a set threshold by a chosen ratio, narrowing its dynamic range.
example: A 4:1 compressor turns 8 dB over threshold into 2 dB over.

definition: A dynamics processor that mutes or strongly reduces a signal when it falls below a threshold, removing spill and noise between notes.
example: A gate on a tom mic cuts the cymbal spill between hits.

definition: A control that sends an adjustable copy of a channel to a separate aux bus, used for monitor mixes and effects. Sends can be pre- or post-fader.
example: Aux 1 feeds the singer's wedge; aux 5 feeds the reverb.

definition: Taken before the channel fader, so the send level does not change when the fader moves. Used for monitor mixes.
example: A pre-fader monitor send stays the same when the FOH engineer rides the vocal.

definition: Taken after the channel fader, so the send follows fader moves. Used for effects like reverb, so wet and dry stay in proportion.
example: Pull the vocal fader down and its post-fader reverb send fades too.

definition: A separate mix sent to the performers so they can hear themselves, through floor wedges, side fills or in-ear monitors. Usually fed from pre-fader aux sends.
example: The drummer's monitor mix is mostly kick, bass and click.

definition: Placing a mono signal between the left and right of a stereo mix with the pan control.
example: Panning a synth pad 30% left makes room for a guitar on the right.

definition: A sliding level control on a mixer, setting a channel's or bus's level in the mix. Its unity mark (0 dB) passes the signal unchanged.
example: Keep faders near 0 dB so there is travel both ways.

definition: Choosing where a signal goes: which buses, groups and outputs a channel feeds.
example: Route all drum channels to subgroup 1.

definition: A point in a mixer where several signals are summed, such as the main L/R mix, an aux bus or a subgroup.
example: The main stereo bus feeds the PA.

definition: A bus that sums related channels (all drums, all backing vocals) to one fader, so a section can be controlled or processed together.
example: Compress the whole drum subgroup with one compressor.

definition: A control group where one master fader remotely sets the levels of member channels without summing their audio. Named after the voltage-controlled amplifiers that did this in analogue desks.
example: Pull the drums VCA down 3 dB and every drum channel drops 3 dB.

definition: The digital-console equivalent of a VCA group: one fader controls the levels of member channels without summing audio.
example: A DCA for backing vocals lets you ride all three singers at once.

definition: Setting the level at each stage of a signal chain so the signal stays well above the noise floor and well below clipping everywhere.
example: Good gain staging starts with the preamp, not the master fader.

definition: A gain of 1 (0 dB): output equals input.
example: Set outboard gear to unity so it neither boosts nor cuts.

definition: External hardware processors (compressors, EQs, effects) connected to a mixer, outside the console itself.
example: A rack of outboard gear patched into the inserts.

definition: How far a signal is above the noise floor, in decibels. Higher is cleaner.
example: A signal at +4 dBu over a −86 dBu noise floor has a 90 dB signal-to-noise ratio.

definition: Decibels relative to full scale: digital level where 0 dBFS is the largest possible value, so all real levels are negative.
example: Nominal levels around −18 dBFS leave headroom for peaks.

definition: Voltage level in decibels relative to 0.775 V RMS. Professional line level is +4 dBu (about 1.23 V RMS).
